# Docker deployment configuration (copy to .env)
# The image is built locally by `docker compose build`; there is no registry tag.
# Address the web UI is published on. 127.0.0.1 keeps it host-local; set 0.0.0.0
# to reach it from another machine or from Windows when HIVE runs inside WSL.
HIVE_BIND_ADDR=127.0.0.1
# Reverse proxies (comma-separated CIDRs) whose X-Forwarded-For the login rate
# limit trusts. Empty: the header is ignored. See "Reverse proxy deployment" in README.md.
HIVE_TRUSTED_PROXIES=
# Optional key for the secrets encrypted in the database (32 bytes, base64 or hex,
# e.g. `openssl rand -base64 32`). Empty: keys/secret.key, generated at first start.
# Set it when ./keys is not persistent. Losing the key loses the stored secrets.
# HIVE_SECRET_KEY=
POSTGRES_USER=hive
POSTGRES_PASSWORD=change-me-please
POSTGRES_DB=hive

# LLM (fill one or both; you can also leave empty and configure in the UI)
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=
OPENAI_API_KEY=
HIVE_LLM_PROVIDER=
HIVE_LLM_MODEL=
HIVE_LLM_BASE_URL=
HIVE_LLM_PROXY=

# Untrusted-output boundary. Frames every tool output between nonce-tagged markers so
# the model treats it as data, not instructions. On by default (unset or empty = on);
# set HIVE_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0 (or false/off/no) to disable it. Measured cost: about
# 154 bytes per tool result plus one system note.
# HIVE_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0

# Noise profile of the requests HIVE sends to targets (WebFetch, http custom tools, enrich
# probe). Default off: no limit, requests unchanged. quiet = 2 req/s per host, burst 4,
# 1 in flight; balanced = 5 req/s, burst 10, 2 in flight; aggressive = 20 req/s, burst 40,
# 4 in flight. A profile also adds jitter, backs off on 429/503 and merges identical GETs
# of one task per tool (short cache; WebFetch is paced only). Bash-launched tools are not throttled.
# HIVE_NOISE_PROFILE=balanced
# User-Agent set on target requests that have none, only under a profile. Empty = unchanged.
# HIVE_TARGET_USER_AGENT=

# Run budgets (optional). Unset or 0 = unlimited, nothing changes. TASK_* caps a whole task
# (planner rounds and all its workers); INTENT_* caps one worker run. Kept in memory: a
# restart, or a revive of a finished task, starts a fresh budget.
# Below 50000 tokens a task gets no worker at all (one worker costs about 50000 tokens by
# default); from 50000 to about 70000 it typically gets one worker, then the forced wrap-up. Use a
# budget well above 70000 for real exploration.
# HIVE_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS=
# HIVE_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS=
# HIVE_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS=
# HIVE_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS=

# Update banner (optional). HIVE_UPDATE_CHECK=1 lets the backend check the public GitHub
# releases API for a newer HIVE release at most once per 24 h and show a dismissible banner.
# Off by default: unset, no update request is made.
# HIVE_UPDATE_CHECK=1

FILE: .github/scripts/bot.sh
=====================================================================
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Lightweight triage and reply bot for issues and pull requests.
# Runs inside GitHub Actions; no server involved.
#
# Triggers (see bot.yml):
#   - issue opened: exactly one triage comment per issue
#   - comment containing @hive-bot: answers that comment (works in PR
#     threads too, since issue_comment fires there)
#   - pull request opened: one first-look review comment
# The bot never posts an approving review and never replies to itself,
# to the maintainer, or to other bots (enforced in bot.yml).
set -uo pipefail

MAX_CHARS=8000
FOOTER='---
🤖 automated reply from the repo bot. A human maintainer reads everything. Ping me in any comment with `@hive-bot`.'

log() { echo "[bot] $*"; }

[ -z "${DEEPSEEK_API_KEY:-}" ] && { log "DEEPSEEK_API_KEY secret is not set; skipping."; exit 0; }

ev=$(cat "$GITHUB_EVENT_PATH")
event_name="$GITHUB_EVENT_NAME"
repo="$GITHUB_REPOSITORY"

ask_model() { # $1 = system prompt, $2 = user payload, $3 = "json" for JSON mode; prints the answer
  local body="${2:0:$MAX_CHARS}" extra
  local req resp
  extra='{}'
  [ "${3:-}" = "json" ] && extra='{ "response_format": { "type": "json_object" } }'
  req=$(jq -n --arg sys "$1" --arg body "$body" --argjson extra "$extra" \
    '{model: "deepseek-flash",
      messages: [{role: "system", content: $sys}, {role: "user", content: $body}],
      max_tokens: 900, temperature: 0} * $extra')
  resp=$(curl -sS --max-time 120 https://api.deepseek.com/chat/completions \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEEPSEEK_API_KEY" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d "$req")
  if ! jq -e '.choices[0].message.content' <<<"$resp" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    log "api call failed, raw response: ${resp:0:300}"
    echo ""
    return
  fi
  jq -r '.choices[0].message.content' <<<"$resp"
}

repo_context() { git ls-files | head -120; }

post_comment() { # $1 = issue or PR number, $2 = markdown text
  { echo "$2"; echo; echo "$FOOTER"; } > /tmp/bot-comment.md
  if gh issue view "$1" --json pull_request --jq '.pull_request' | grep -q .; then
    gh pr comment "$1" --body-file /tmp/bot-comment.md
  else
    gh issue comment "$1" --body-file /tmp/bot-comment.md
  fi
}

eyes() { # $1 = issue or PR number
  gh api -X POST "repos/$repo/issues/$1/reactions" -f content=eyes >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
}

# Labels the triage may request; anything else the model names is dropped.
LABEL_COLORS=(bug=d73a4a question=d876e3 feature=a2eeef P1=b60205 P2=fbca04 P3=c5def5)

ensure_label() { # $1 = label name
  local entry color
  for entry in "${LABEL_COLORS[@]}"; do
    [ "${entry%%=*}" = "$1" ] && color="${entry#*=}"
  done
  gh label create "$1" --color "${color:-cccccc}" --force >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
}

apply_labels() { # $1 = issue number, $2 = comma separated label names from the model
  local wanted=() item ok w
  IFS=',' read -ra parts <<<"$2"
  for item in "${parts[@]}"; do
    item=$(echo "$item" | tr -d '[:space:]' | tr '[:upper:]' '[:lower:]')
    ok=0
    for w in bug question feature p1 p2 p3; do [ "$item" = "$w" ] && ok=1; done
    [ "$ok" = 1 ] || continue
    case "$item" in p1|p2|p3) item=${item^^} ;; esac
    wanted+=("$item")
  done
  if [ "${#wanted[@]}" -gt 0 ]; then
    for item in "${wanted[@]}"; do ensure_label "$item"; done
    gh issue edit "$1" --add-label "$(IFS=,; echo "${wanted[*]}")" >/dev/null 2>&1 || log "label apply failed"
    log "applied labels: ${wanted[*]}"
  fi
}

already_triaged() { # $1 = issue number
  gh api "repos/$repo/issues/$1/comments" --jq '.[].body' 2>/dev/null \
    | grep -q 'automated reply from the repo bot'
}

answer=""

case "$event_name" in
  issues)
    number=$(jq -r '.issue.number' <<<"$ev")
    title=$(jq -r '.issue.title' <<<"$ev")
    body=$(jq -r '.issue.body // ""' <<<"$ev")
    maintainer_opened=false
    [ "$GITHUB_ACTOR" = "BaaRai" ] && maintainer_opened=true
    if [ "$maintainer_opened" = false ] && already_triaged "$number"; then log "issue #$number already triaged"; exit 0; fi
    [ "$maintainer_opened" = false ] && eyes "$number"
    answer=$(ask_model \
      'You are the triage bot of an open-source Go + Next.js repository (an autonomous penetration testing agent system; AGPL-3.0). Respond ONLY with a single JSON object, no markdown, no prose outside the JSON, exactly of this shape: {"comment": "<your triage comment, max 180 words, same language as the report>", "labels": ["<zero or more of: bug, question, feature, P1, P2, P3>"]}. Classify the report as bug, question, or feature request; if it is a question, answer it concisely using the repository file list as context in the comment; if it is a bug report, the comment says what reproduction steps or version information are missing; if it is a feature request, the comment restates it in one sentence; add a priority label (P1 security impact or data loss, P2 core functionality broken, P3 minor or cosmetic) only for bugs; use an empty labels array if nothing fits.' \
      "Issue title: $title

Issue body:
$body

Repository file list:
$(repo_context)" json)
    [ -z "$answer" ] && { log "model returned nothing"; exit 0; }
    log "raw json: $answer"
    comment=$(jq -r '.comment // empty' <<<"$answer" 2>/dev/null)
    reply_labels=$(jq -r 'if (.labels | type) == "array" then (.labels | map(tostring) | join(",")) else "" end' <<<"$answer" 2>/dev/null)
    [ -z "$reply_labels" ] && reply_labels="none"
    log "parsed labels: $reply_labels"
    if [ "$maintainer_opened" = true ]; then
      log "maintainer issue #$number: labels only, staying silent"
      apply_labels "$number" "$reply_labels"
      exit 0
    fi
    if [ -n "$comment" ]; then
      post_comment "$number" "$comment"
    else
      log "no comment field in JSON; labels only"
    fi
    apply_labels "$number" "$reply_labels"
    ;;

  issue_comment)
    number=$(jq -r '.issue.number' <<<"$ev")
    body=$(jq -r '.comment.body' <<<"$ev")
    question="${body#*@hive-bot}"            # strip up to the mention
    echo "$body" | grep -qi '@hive-bot' || { log "no mention; skipping"; exit 0; }
    eyes "$number"
    answer=$(ask_model \
      'You are the helper bot of an open-source Go + Next.js repository (an autonomous penetration testing agent system; AGPL-3.0). Someone pinged you with a question about this repository. Answer it concisely and only from what the repository file list suggests; say plainly when you are not sure and suggest opening a proper issue. Maximum 180 words, plain markdown, reply in the language of the question.' \
      "Question:
$question

Repository file list:
$(repo_context)")
    [ -z "$answer" ] && { log "model returned nothing"; exit 0; }
    post_comment "$number" "$answer"
    ;;

  pull_request)
    number=$(jq -r '.pull_request.number' <<<"$ev")
    title=$(jq -r '.pull_request.title' <<<"$ev")
    body=$(jq -r '.pull_request.body // ""' <<<"$ev")
    eyes "$number"
    diff=$(gh pr diff "$number" 2>/dev/null | head -c 4000)
    answer=$(ask_model \
      'You are the first-look bot of an open-source Go + Next.js repository (an autonomous penetration testing agent system; AGPL-3.0). Summarize what this pull request changes in two or three sentences, then a short checklist: does it include or update tests, does it touch documentation where needed, does anything look inconsistent with the described goal. You are commenting for information only; you do not approve or request changes. Maximum 180 words, plain markdown.' \
      "Pull request title: $title

Pull request description:
$body

Diff (truncated):
$diff")
    [ -z "$answer" ] && { log "model returned nothing"; exit 0; }
    post_comment "$number" "$answer"
    ;;

  *)
    log "unhandled event $event_name; skipping"
    ;;
esac

log "done"

=====================================================================
FILE: .github/workflows/bot.yml
=====================================================================
name: bot

on:
  issues:
    types: [opened]
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
  pull_request:
    types: [opened]

permissions:
  issues: write
  pull-requests: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  reply:
    # Issue opening is always handled (the maintainer gets silent labeling,
    # visitors get the full triage). Comments and PRs serve visitors only:
    # never react to the maintainer, to bots, or to itself.
    if: >
      github.event_name == 'issues' ||
      (github.actor != 'ProjectZeroDays' &&
       github.actor != 'github-actions[bot]' &&
       github.actor != 'dependabot[bot]')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: triage or reply
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          GITHUB_EVENT_PATH: ${{ github.event_path }}
          DEEPSEEK_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEEPSEEK_API_KEY }}
        run: bash .github/scripts/bot.sh

FILE: .github/workflows/ci.yml
=====================================================================
name: ci

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  go:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: hive
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass
          POSTGRES_DB: hivetest
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U hive"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 10
    env:
      HIVE_PG_DSN: postgres://hive:testpass@localhost:5432/hivetest?sslmode=disable
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v5
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod
      - run: go build ./...
      - run: go vet ./...
      # Skipped tests, tracked in issue #9:
      # - TestGraphOverviewExpandsAssociatedCompanyScope,
      #   TestCaptureApprovalLifecycle: fail on unmodified upstream code with a
      #   fresh database.
      # - TestSideUsageRecordedOnceOnConsumerCancellation: concurrency/cancellation
      #   test that passes locally but is timing-sensitive on 2-core CI runners.
      # They now skip themselves in code (t.Skip with a pointer to the issue).
      - name: go test
        # -p 1: package test suites share the single postgres service; running
        # them in parallel makes packages delete each other's rows (observed
        # as rotating failures in the agent package). Serial package execution
        # keeps the database state deterministic.
        run: go test -p 1 ./...
      - name: go test -race
        # Race detector on the packages that pass under -race today. ./server
        # joined once its suite was checked with -race against postgres and its
        # test teardown fixed (#227, #228).
        # Its own database: the plain run above leaves rows behind and the db tests
        # are not idempotent across runs (duplicate llm_profiles names).
        env:
          HIVE_PG_DSN: postgres://hive:testpass@localhost:5432/hivetest_race?sslmode=disable

        run: >-
          go test -race -p 1 ./agent ./cmd/hive ./config ./db ./evidence ./guard
          ./intercept ./llmpool ./llmrec ./mcphttp ./notify ./server ./sidequestion
          ./traffic

  shell:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      # shellcheck is preinstalled on the ubuntu runners. -S warning: the scripts
      # currently have only info-level notes (intentional A && B || C chains in
      # update.sh, an unquoted glob in backup.sh's prune), so fail on warnings.
      - run: shellcheck -S warning install.sh update.sh start.sh scripts/backup.sh reset-password.sh scripts/extract-changelog-section.sh scripts/test-extract-changelog-section.sh
      - run: bash scripts/test-extract-changelog-section.sh

  web:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: web
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: web/package-lock.json
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit
      - run: npm run build:static

FILE: .github/workflows/release.yml
=====================================================================
name: release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*"]
  # Dry run: builds, SBOM, attestations and workflow artifacts only. The GitHub
  # Release and the image push are gated on github.event_name == 'push'.
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: write # required to create the Release

jobs:
  # ① Frontend static export (once), reused by the cross-compiled platform builds
  frontend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: web/package-lock.json
      - run: npm ci
        working-directory: web
      - run: npm run build:static
        working-directory: web
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: web-dist
          path: web/out

  # ② Cross-compile for five platforms (with embedded frontend) + zip packaging
  binaries:
    needs: frontend
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        include:
          - { goos: linux, goarch: amd64 }
          - { goos: linux, goarch: arm64 }
          - { goos: darwin, goarch: amd64 }
          - { goos: darwin, goarch: arm64 }
          - { goos: windows, goarch: amd64 }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v5
        with:
          go-version: "1.26"
          cache: true
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: web-dist
          path: server/webui/dist
      - name: Build and package with build.sh
        env:
          HIVE_TARGET_OS: ${{ matrix.goos }}
          HIVE_TARGET_ARCH: ${{ matrix.goarch }}
          HIVE_BUILD_VERSION: ${{ github.ref_name }}
          HIVE_SKIP_FRONTEND: "1"
          HIVE_SKIP_NPM_CI: "1"
          # UPX self-extracting ELF binaries crash on some Linux kernels, virtualization
          # setups, and security policies. Releases use Go linker trimming and zip
          # compression, prioritizing portability.
          HIVE_COMPRESS: "0"
          HIVE_PACKAGE: "1"
          HIVE_PACKAGE_DIR: dist
        run: |
          ./build.sh --target "${HIVE_TARGET_OS}/${HIVE_TARGET_ARCH}"
      - name: Smoke test Linux amd64 binary
        if: matrix.goos == 'linux' && matrix.goarch == 'amd64'
        run: dist/hive-linux-amd64/hive -h
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: pkg-${{ matrix.goos }}-${{ matrix.goarch }}
          path: "dist/*.zip"
      # Upload raw Linux binaries separately for reuse by the docker job (avoids rebuilding the frontend + Go inside the image)
      - if: matrix.goos == 'linux'
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: bin-linux-${{ matrix.goarch }}
          path: dist/hive-linux-${{ matrix.goarch }}/hive

  # ③ Collect all zips → create the GitHub Release
  release:
    needs: binaries
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write # create the Release (softprops/action-gh-release)
      id-token: write # Sigstore signing of the provenance attestation
      attestations: write # store the attestation on the repository
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4 # CHANGELOG.md and the extractor script
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          pattern: pkg-*
          merge-multiple: true
          path: dist
      - name: Generate checksums
        working-directory: dist
        run: sha256sum *.zip > SHA256SUMS
      # SBOM of what ships: the Go modules embedded in the linux/amd64 binary, plus
      # the frontend lockfile and the Go module files.
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: bin-linux-amd64
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/sbom-src/bin
      - uses: anchore/sbom-action/download-syft@66cbf4bc1f1c0d2edc94016e65bc221b6bb0ad6c # v0.24.3
        id: syft
        with:
          syft-version: v1.54.0
      - name: Generate CycloneDX SBOM
        env:
          SYFT: ${{ steps.syft.outputs.cmd }}
          SRC: ${{ runner.temp }}/sbom-src
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          mkdir -p "$SRC/web"
          cp go.mod go.sum "$SRC/"
          cp web/package-lock.json "$SRC/web/"
          sbom="dist/hive-${TAG}.cdx.json"
          "$SYFT" scan "dir:$SRC" --source-name hive --source-version "$TAG" -o "cyclonedx-json=$sbom"
          grep -q '"pkg:golang/' "$sbom" || { echo "::error::SBOM has no pkg:golang entries"; exit 1; }
          grep -q '"pkg:npm/' "$sbom" || { echo "::error::SBOM has no pkg:npm entries"; exit 1; }
          echo "SBOM_PATH=$sbom" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - uses: actions/attest-build-provenance@4d101475d8b20a2381f78447822ac1eab6504dd8 # v4.2.2
        with:
          subject-path: dist/*.zip
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: release-metadata
          path: |
            dist/SHA256SUMS
            ${{ env.SBOM_PATH }}
      - name: Release body from CHANGELOG.md
        env:
          TAG: ${{ github.ref_name }}
        run: |
          version="${TAG#v}"
          if bash scripts/extract-changelog-section.sh "$version" CHANGELOG.md > "$RUNNER_TEMP/release-body.md"; then
            echo "Release body: CHANGELOG.md section [$version]"
          else
            echo "::warning::CHANGELOG.md has no section [$version]; using the generic release body"
            echo "Release $TAG. See CHANGELOG.md for the list of changes in this release." > "$RUNNER_TEMP/release-body.md"
          fi
      - uses: softprops/action-gh-release@v2
        if: github.event_name == 'push'
        with:
          files: |
            dist/*.zip
            dist/SHA256SUMS
            ${{ env.SBOM_PATH }}
          generate_release_notes: false
          body_path: ${{ runner.temp }}/release-body.md

  # ④ Multi-arch image → push to Docker Hub (reuses the Linux binaries built by the
  #    binaries job; the image only installs tools + ships the binary; arm64 only needs
  #    to emulate the apt layer, so builds are much faster)
  # Publishing the image needs Docker Hub credentials and a namespace we own, so the
  # job stays skipped unless the repository defines DOCKERHUB_ENABLED (set it to true
  # and provide DOCKERHUB_USERNAME / DOCKERHUB_TOKEN secrets plus DOCKERHUB_IMAGE).
  docker:
    needs: binaries
    if: ${{ vars.DOCKERHUB_ENABLED == 'true' && github.event_name == 'push' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4 # fetch the Dockerfile and skills/
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: bin-linux-amd64
          path: dist/amd64
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: bin-linux-arm64
          path: dist/arm64
      - uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v3
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/metadata-action@v5
        id: meta
        with:
          images: ${{ vars.DOCKERHUB_IMAGE }}
          tags: |
            type=ref,event=tag
            type=raw,value=latest
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

FILE: .opencode/command/CIAHiveSkilCreator.md
=====================================================================
---
description: Execute the next queued Hive build part, or a named part by number
agent: build
---

You are executing one part of a staged build for the Hive app.

$ARGUMENTS may be: empty (next pending part), a number, `status`, or `skip <n>`.

.opencode/hive/QUEUE.md is the single source of truth. One line per part:
07 | pending | extensibility install surface
States: pending, active, done, blocked, skipped. Only one part may be active.

Rules:
1. One part per invocation. Never start the next.
2. Read only the part file plus what it names. No out-of-scope refactors.
3. State the plan in three lines or fewer, then execute.
4. Run the suite and the build after editing. Both green or the part stays active.
5. Commit as hive(<part>): <summary>.
6. Set the part done, append a one-line note to .opencode/hive/NOTES.md with anything the next part must know.
7. If blocked, set blocked, write the reason, stop. Do not improvise around it.

Never: batch two parts in one commit, mark done on a red build, skip tests as trivial, cross the phase boundary.

Part files live at .opencode/hive/parts/NN-slug.md. If missing, stop and say so.

# Hive Build Notes

## 2026-11-24 — Part 02 shipped

Commit on `main` — `hive(02): rebrand product surface to Hive`.

**Scope decision:** product-surface rename only. User-visible strings (app config/title/copyright, login + setup pages incl. Terms of Use dialog, sidebar alt text, update toast, logs sample, notify help/placeholders, report template title, guard/intercept platform-control prefix `[Hive platform control, not target defense]`, startup log line, README/SECURITY prose) now say **Hive**. Login/setup also switched from the old `logo.png` silhouette to the `cia2.png` seal already used in the sidebar.

**Deliberately left as ARTEX (contract, not brand):**
- Login username `ARTEX` + JWT subject (`server/auth.go`) — auth contract, part 11 reworks it.
- Storage keys: `artex_token` cookie/localStorage, `artex_*` preference keys.
- Env vars (`ARTEX_CONFIG`, `ARTEX_PG_DSN`, `ARTEX_KEY_DIR`, `ARTEX_NOTIFY_ALLOW_LOCAL`, budgets, etc.).
- Binary name `artex`, systemd unit, docker container `artex-pg`, repo paths, Go module path.
- Upstream URLs: BaaRai/ARTEX badges, releases feed, clone/install commands, SECURITY advisory channel.
- `server/intercept_live_test.go` fixture string (live-gated, wording differs, tests pass-through).

**Verified:** `tsc --noEmit` clean; biome findings on login page are pre-existing `useSortedClasses` nursery noise on untouched lines; `go test ./guard/ ./intercept/` green (tests assert the renamed constant).

**Ops:** the llama-server runner wedged again (99% CPU, 3.8GB RSS, swap 3/4 full) and OOM-killed `tsc`. Fix per part-01 notes: `kill -9 <llama-server pid>`; ollama.service stays active and respawns a runner on next request. Build needs the freed memory.

## 2026-11-23 — Part 01 shipped

Commit `a63a225` — `hive(01): repair model pool resolution and fallback`.

**Hardcoded model id audit (spec step 1):**
- `agent/provider.go` (8 sites): env-overridable defaults `gpt-4o`, `gpt-5`, `llama3.2`, `claude-opus-4-8` in `ConfigFromEnv`/`ConfigFrom`. Not pool ids; left.
- `ollama-setup.sh`, `/root/init_install.sh`: `OLLAMA_MODEL` default — already the corrected full hf.co id.
- `llmpool/catalog.go` `LegacyAliases`: the fix itself.
- No planner/pool code hardcodes a model id; profiles come from the DB.

**Verified live:**
- Boot pass surfaced the OpenRouter BYOK restriction as an actionable error naming `https://openrouter.ai/workspaces/default/byok` (journal, 14:59).
- Live pool run (`LIVE_POOL=1`, gated test `llmpool/live_test.go`): BYOK 404 → breaker trip with profile/model/status → failover to ollama → real completion: `reply="OK" via=end_turn tokens={in:21 out:2}` in 264.7s (cold runner load dominates; CPU-bound box).

**Environment notes:**
- 7 GB RAM box; llama-server (pid 95588, port 43357) holds ~3.1 GB and spins a core at ~98% continuously. Go builds OOM unless `-p 1` and orphaned `compile` procs are killed first.
- `go build` needs `-tags embedui` for a usable binary; `./build.sh` does it end-to-end.
- UI login is JWT (`POST /api/auth/login`, username hardcoded `ARTEX`); the DB DSN + key dir for the gated live test: `ARTEX_PG_DSN` from config.json database block, `ARTEX_KEY_DIR=/root/ARTEX` (secret.key lives there).

**Left for later parts:**
- openrouter/free profile is account-side BYOK-restricted — user must attach provider keys or switch profile; error now says so.

**Ops lessons:**
- llama-server can wedge into a 97%-CPU spin with an expired slot; symptom: ollama accepts but never dispatches. Fix: kill the runner, and if the ollama queue itself is stale, `systemctl restart ollama.service`.
- `pkill -f llmpool.test` also matches the wrapping bash -c (the pattern string is in its own cmdline) and SIGKILLs your own exec shell. Use `pkill -f 'llmpool[.]test'`.
- Model slot keep-alive is ~5 min (`--load-mode none`); idle pools pay a multi-minute cold load on this box.
- 02 (deep rename, second pass): module path → github.com/ProjectZeroDays/edg-hive; binary/service/dir/docker/db all hive-named; ARTEX_* env mirrored by server/legacy.go init; artex_* browser storage copied forward by web/src/lib/legacy.ts (wired in api.ts getToken); legacy artex_token cookie still accepted. Product grep for artex now returns only those two migration files. Box: /root/ARTEX → /root/HIVE, hive.service (artex.service removed), container hive-pg, DB user+name hive (269 tables preserved). Suite green, build clean, service live on 8787.

# PHASE 1 — Foundation

## Role
Senior full-stack engineer and product architect, full repo access. Production-grade code.

## Objective
Fix the model pool, rebrand to **Hive**, establish the design system, build auth, accounts, messaging, diagnostics and lifecycle tooling. No network stack, no release.

(Full spec: sections 1–18 as supplied by operator. Key constraints: diff reviewable, preserve existing features, no TODO stubs, ask before destructive migrations. Phase 1 done-when list governs.)

 --accent:#ff3e3e; --accent-hover:#ff5c5c; --accent-tint:rgba(255,62,62,.12);

## Skill format (reference for part 08)

```markdown
---
name: port-sweep
description: Fast TCP port sweep of an in-scope host before enumeration.
version: 1.0.0
tags: [recon, tcp]
---

## When to use
Before service fingerprinting, on any host in scope.

## Steps
1. Run nmap -Pn -p- --min-rate 2000 against the target.
2. Feed open ports to the fingerprint step.

## Notes
Back off to 500 if the target rate-limits.
```

## Liability disclosure (Version 1)

BEFORE YOU START — You are being given a child account on a shared instance run by one admin.

KEYS AND COST: Use your own provider keys where you have them. Keys are yours and the spend is yours. Hosted models are metered against a cap the admin sets and can be withdrawn at any time.

WHAT YOU RUN IS YOURS: Prompts, agent output, and anything the agents do to a target are your responsibility. The admin does not warrant that a scan, exploit, or generated command is correct, safe, or in scope. Verify before you point anything at production.

WHAT THE ADMIN CAN SEE: Request counts, token usage, model used, cost, your logs, and your conversations with the AI. Conversations with the admin are private to the two of you.

NO WARRANTY: Provided as-is. No guarantee of uptime, data retention, or recovery.

By continuing you accept full responsibility for the actions of any agent you start, on any system, and confirm you have permission to test what you point them at.

[ ] I have read and accept Version 1 — recorded with timestamp and IP

# 01 — LLM pool repair

**Goal:** Planner stops 404ing. Roles never run dry.

**Steps**
1. Grep every hardcoded model id, list them in the commit body.
2. Resolve ids against live provider catalogs at boot.
3. Provider prefix normalization plus alias map for legacy ids.
4. Per-role fallback chain with a validation call before use.
5. 404 re-resolves; 429/5xx retries with backoff and jitter.
6. Detect the OpenRouter BYOK restriction, return an actionable error naming key and limit.
7. Log failing id, provider, status.

**Done when**
- Planner run completes on a healthy pool; mocked 404 recovers; empty pool names a reason; BYOK restriction surfaces the fix.

**Commit:** `hive(01): repair model pool resolution and fallback`

# 03 — Design system

**Goal:** Themed tokens, no hardcoded colors.

**Steps**
1. Tokens, light: accent `#1a56db`, hover `#1445b3`, bg `#ffffff`, pane `#f4f4f7`, sidebar `#ececf0`, border `#dcdce4`, text `#1c1b22`, muted `#5c5a63`.
2. Tokens, dark: accent `#ff3e3e`, hover `#ff5c5c`, tint `rgba(255,62,62,.12)`, bg `#1c1b22`, pane `#1a1920`, sidebar `#141319`, card `#434042`, panel `#262530`, border `#4e4b4e`, text `#eceaf0`, muted `#c3bfc7`.
3. `data-theme` on root, persisted, honoring system preference.
4. Accent only on: primary fill, secondary outline, active nav rail, selected row, focus rings, tab rules, non-zero counters, toggles, chart series, destructive text. Nothing else.
5. Tooltips on every icon-only control, nav item, card and widget: 400 ms delay, card bubble, `aria-describedby`, suppressed on touch.
6. Typography: UI Inter, code IBM Plex Mono, terminal JetBrainsMono Nerd Font Mono, bundled with fallbacks.
7. Seal asset fixed across themes.

**Done when**
- Both themes render with zero hardcoded colors; accent coverage under 10% of pixels; tooltips reachable by keyboard.

**Commit:** `hive(03): design system and tokens`

FILE: .opencode/hive/parts/12-invite-tokens.md
=====================================================================
# 12 — Invite tokens

**Goal:** Gated registration.

**Steps**
1. `hive_inv_` + 32 random bytes, base32; store SHA-256 only, show once.
2. Fields: label, max_uses, expires_at, revoke, created_by.
3. Redemption at `/register?token=`, validated and decremented in one transaction.
4. Timing-safe compare, generic error, 5/min/IP, audited.
5. Admin page with uses left, expiry, revoke, copy.

**Done when**
- Concurrent redemption never overshoots max_uses.

**Commit:** `hive(12): invite tokens`

# 32 — Local subnet scan

**Goal:** Reach the LAN when hosted locally.

**Steps**
1. Detect interface and subnet mask.
2. Bind to LAN, accept RFC1918 CIDR, refuse targets outside the subnet unless overridden.

**Done when**
- The subnet is detected correctly and out-of-range targets are refused.

# ARTEX

**Autonomous penetration testing that keeps its receipts.**

Self-hosted multi-agent offensive security. A planner explores, workers run real tools,
and every finding stays bound to the assets and HTTP traffic that prove it.

[![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/BaaRai/ARTEX?label=release&color=6b34db)](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/releases)
[![License](https://img.shields.io/github/license/BaaRai/ARTEX?color=6b34db)](LICENSE)
[![CI](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg?branch=main)](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![Go](https://img.shields.io/github/go-mod/go-version/BaaRai/ARTEX?color=6b34db)](go.mod)

[Quick start](#quick-start) · [Screenshots](#screenshots) · [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Install](#installation) · [Configuration](#configuration) · [Security](SECURITY.md)

</div>

---

ARTEX is a self-hosted, LLM-driven penetration testing platform. It is not a chat wrapper around
a scanner: a planner splits a goal into intents, workers execute them with real tools, and the
results are written back into **two linked graphs**: one for what you know about the target, one
for how the test is progressing. Every finding can carry the captured request and response that
justify it, and every autonomous action passes through scope rules, approval gates and budgets.

- **It explores, it doesn't chat.** Goal decomposition, intent dispatch, worker execution and
  write-back form a closed loop that keeps advancing until the goal is proven.
- **Two graphs, one audit trail.** The shared asset graph says *what exists*; the per-task
  exploration graph says *what was tried, what it produced, and why*. Anchors link the two.
- **Findings with evidence.** A recording MITM proxy and a browser extension capture real traffic;
  findings, evidence quotes and retests are tied to the exact request/response.
- **Autonomy with brakes.** Human-in-the-loop approvals, argv-prefix rules, scope/deny gates,
  token and turn budgets, a target noise governor, and prompt-injection framing on tool output.
- **Self-hosted and model-agnostic.** One Go binary with the Next.js UI embedded, PostgreSQL,
  your own Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or a local Ollama.

---

## Quick start

```bash
git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git
cd ARTEX
cp .env.example .env            # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD (and optionally an LLM key)
docker compose up -d --build    # builds from this checkout, starts PostgreSQL
```

Open **http://localhost:8787**. On the first visit `/setup` asks for the one-time setup token
printed at startup:

```bash
docker compose logs artex | grep "Setup token"
```

> There is no prebuilt Docker image to pull: the image is always built from your checkout.
> For all installation paths (script, binaries, source, release archives), see [Installation](#installation).

## How it works

### Dual-graph architecture: exploration graph + asset graph

ARTEX separates *what the goals are* from *how far testing has progressed* into two independent
graphs linked by anchors:

- **Asset graph (shared across tasks).** One source of truth for `root_domain / subdomain / ip /
  service / app / endpoint`, owned by companies. Parent-child relationships and deduplication keys
  are computed by the program; agents only submit raw observations.
- **Exploration graph (per task).** The task's reasoning and progress: `goal / intent / fact /
  finding / hint` nodes connected by `spawns / derived_from / yields / proves` edges into a lineage
  chain.
- **Anchors link them.** `exploration_anchors(node_id, asset_id)` ties intents, facts and findings
  to concrete assets: which assets a direction touched, and which intents tested a given asset.
  This also powers **asset test coverage** and the coverage graph.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph EG["Exploration graph (per-task · advance chain)"]
    direction TB
    G["goal"]
    I1["intent A"]
    F1["fact"]
    I2["intent B"]
    FD["finding (vulnerability)"]
    G -->|spawns| I1
    I1 -->|yields| F1
    F1 -->|derived_from| I2
    I2 -->|proves| FD
  end
  subgraph AG["Asset graph (globally shared · source of truth)"]
    direction TB
    RD["root_domain"]
    SD["subdomain"]
    SV["service"]
    EP["endpoint"]
    RD --> SD --> SV --> EP
  end
  I1 -. anchor .-> SD
  F1 -. anchor .-> SV
  I2 -. anchor .-> EP
  FD -. anchor .-> EP
```

The **planner** reads the exploration graph, judges goals, and dispatches intents only when there
is an uncovered direction; a **worker** claims one intent, executes it, writes assets/facts/findings
back into both graphs, then stops.

### The engine loop

The engine is event-driven: any graph change wakes the planner, workers claim and execute intents,
write-back triggers the next round, until `prove_goal` closes the task.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  participant EV as graph-change debounce
  participant P as planner
  participant FR as frontier intent queue
  participant W as worker
  participant PX as recording proxy
  participant DB as dual graphs + activity

  EV-->>P: wake up
  P->>DB: read situation (graph_overview prefetch + coverage/scope)
  P->>FR: dispatch 0..N intents (with asset_ids)
  Note over P,FR: most wake-ups dispatch 0 (no new direction means done)
  W->>FR: claimNext claims one intent
  W->>DB: fetch the raw assets of the intent's asset_ids
  W->>PX: real tool execution (Kali / Bash / HTTP)
  PX-->>W: response (fully traced + CA verified)
  W->>DB: write back fact / asset / finding + per-step activity
  DB-->>EV: graph change
  EV-->>P: wake again (closed loop)
```

### Durable attack chains, shared worker memory

Real attack chains are multi-step and ordered (find an injection → get credentials → move
laterally). The planner keeps a **todolist retained per task across wake-ups**: it records the
chain once, then dispatches the next step only when its prerequisites are satisfied by facts.

Workers can also **search each other's execution traces** (`search_all_worker_traces`,
`list_worker_traces`, `get_worker_trace`). Observations that never became formal facts (an error
message, a response snippet, a hidden parameter) are still reusable by the next worker, while each
worker remains confined to the intent it claimed.

---

## Features

### Evidence, not chat logs

- **Recording MITM proxy** (`:8788`) with a generated CA: every Bash/HTTP tool call is traced, and
  request/response evidence can be bound to a finding.
- **Browser extension** (`extension/`) for authenticated targets: log in once (captcha, email OTP,
  2FA included), capture the session, and the requests/responses land in the same traffic store.

  <details>
  <summary>Using the traffic capture extension</summary>

  - Load the unpacked extension from `extension/` (Chrome/Edge: Developer Mode → Load unpacked);
  - In the popup, set your ARTEX URL and token, then press **Start capture** on the tab you are
    browsing;
  - Use the site normally; text requests/responses are batched to `POST /api/traffic/ingest`
    (authenticated). Binary bodies (images, fonts) are skipped, bodies are truncated at 256 KiB,
    batches are capped at 50 entries;
  - Press **Stop** when done. Everything stays in your local traffic store.

  </details>
- **Verified findings**: findings carry a POE level, a verification status and a note; a finding is
  `verified` only when a bound proof/response and verbatim evidence quotes support it. Gzip/deflate
  bodies are decoded before the quote check.
- **Vulnerability retest loop**: a dedicated `retester` agent re-runs a finding with optional fixed
  version/conditions, records `Still reproducible / Fixed / Cannot confirm`, and can move the
  finding to `Fixed` automatically. Original evidence and reports are preserved.
- **Reports and exports**: findings, evidence and task archives, with traffic snapshots kept
  encrypted at rest.

### Control without slowing down

- **Interception gate**: every tool call can require human approval, with rules by `string`,
  `regex` or **argv prefix**. An argv rule is a JSON array of 1 to 8 tokens (Bash only, for
  example `["git","push"]`); it matches only a single simple command whose parsed prefix equals
  the pattern exactly. Pipes, lists, redirections, prefix assignments, subshells, background jobs,
  wrapper programs and command/parameter substitutions do not match; flags are ignored by
  construction (`["git","push"]` covers `git push --force`, but `git -C /repo push` matches
  nothing). Each approval records who decided: `human`, `rule`, `model` or `system`.
- **Scope and target gate**: scope rows define the coverage denominator; assets outside the
  declared scope are not explored. The target gate (off by default, API-only) can refuse
  destinations that were not approved.
- **Budgets**: `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS` cap a whole task (planner and
  workers); `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS` cap one worker run. Near the
  limit the task enters a forced wrap-up; a worker is not started when the remaining budget cannot
  cover it. Budgets are in memory: a restart starts fresh.
- **Noise governor**: `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE=quiet|balanced|aggressive` paces requests ARTEX sends to
  targets (per-host rate, burst, in-flight limit, jitter, backoff on 429/503, short GET caching).
  With a profile set, agents also receive low-and-slow flags for the installed scanners.
- **Untrusted-output boundary (on by default)**: tool results are framed between nonce-tagged
  markers so the model treats them as data, not instructions. Disable with
  `ARTEX_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0`.

### Assets and coverage

- **Coverage ledger and force-directed coverage graph**: in-scope assets are highlighted as tested
  or untested, with linked intents, facts and findings per node.
- **Company-scoped asset graph**: shared across tasks, deduplicated by the program, with
  domain → subdomain → service → endpoint containment.
- **ScopeSentry sync**: pull asset data from a
  [ScopeSentry](https://github.com/Autumn-27/ScopeSentry) instance by project or task, merged by
  company scope into the asset graph for agents to explore.

  <details>
  <summary>Syncing from ScopeSentry</summary>

  - On the **Asset Sync** page, enter the ScopeSentry address and API key;
  - Choose the targets and asset types by **project** or **task** (domains / subdomains / IPs /
    ports / sites / endpoints…);
  - Import: rows are merged by company asset scope and become part of the asset graph.

  </details>
- **Task categories, templates, relations and archives** for repeatable engagements.

### Platform

- **LLM profiles with failover**: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenAI-compatible relays and keyless Ollama;
  multiple profiles per task with automatic failover.
- **Token accounting**: per-task and per-session usage, cache reads/writes, and an LLM record view
  for every call.
- **MCP servers, skills, memory and a workspace**: extend the agent with remote tools and reusable
  prompt/playbook material.
- **Single binary**: the Next.js UI is embedded with `go:embed`; PostgreSQL is the only external
  dependency.

---

## Installation

> Requires **PostgreSQL**; exploration requires an **LLM** (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or
> `OPENAI_API_KEY`, also configurable in the UI).

### Option 1: one-click install script (recommended)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git
cd ARTEX
./install.sh
```

The script detects or installs Docker, then offers **① all-Docker** (writes `.env`, runs
`docker compose up -d --build`) or **② local build and run** (generates `config.json`, builds the
embedded binary, starts it).

Open **http://localhost:8787**; `/setup` asks for the one-time setup token printed at startup
(`docker compose logs artex | grep "Setup token"`).

The UI listens on `127.0.0.1` by default. To reach it from another machine (or from Windows when
ARTEX runs inside WSL), set `ARTEX_BIND_ADDR=0.0.0.0` in `.env` (the setup token still protects the
first-run claim), or keep loopback and use a reverse proxy or SSH tunnel.

### Option 2: Docker Compose (manual)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX.git
cd ARTEX
cp .env.example .env            # set POSTGRES_PASSWORD, optionally ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
docker compose up -d --build
# → http://localhost:8787
```

The image includes a scanner toolchain (`nmap`, `nuclei`, `httpx`, `katana`, `ffuf`, `dalfox`,
`sqlmap`, `ripgrep`, `curl`, `npm`, …); `./skills` and `./data` are persisted via bind mounts.

For remote MCP you can choose `http` (Streamable HTTP) or `sse` (legacy SSE) in system settings.
Legacy SSE servers usually establish the event stream with `GET /sse` and receive JSON-RPC over
`/message?sessionId=...`; configure the URL as `/sse` and send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

### Option 3: prebuilt binaries (Releases)

Download the zip for your platform from [Releases](https://github.com/BaaRai/ARTEX/releases). It
contains `artex`, `start.sh` (`start.bat` on Windows), `skills/` and `config.example.json`:

```bash
cp config.example.json config.json   # fill in the database connection
./start.sh                           # → http://localhost:8787
```

Start with `start.sh` / `start.bat`, not `./artex`: it is a daemon script that restarts the process
after a backoff. To keep it in the background: `nohup ./start.sh >artex.log 2>&1 &`.

#### Verifying a release

Each release attaches `SHA256SUMS` and a CycloneDX SBOM, `artex-<tag>.cdx.json` (Go modules in the
linux/amd64 binary, the frontend `package-lock.json`, `go.mod`/`go.sum`), next to the zips. The zips
also carry a GitHub build provenance attestation. Releases published before this was added have
neither.

```bash
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS                           # add --ignore-missing if you downloaded only some zips
gh attestation verify <zip> --repo BaaRai/ARTEX   # built by this repository's release workflow
```

### Option 4: build the single binary from source

```bash
cd web && npm ci && npm run build:static && cd ..
cp -r web/out server/webui/dist
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags embedui -o artex ./cmd/artex
./start.sh
```

Only `-tags embedui` embeds the frontend into the binary.

### Option 5: cross-platform release archives

`build.sh` builds and embeds the frontend, strips debug info, and writes zips for Linux
amd64/arm64, macOS amd64/arm64 and Windows amd64 by default:

```bash
./build.sh --release
# output: dist/artex-<version>-*.zip

ARTEX_TARGETS=linux/amd64,windows/amd64 ./build.sh --release
./build.sh --target linux/amd64 --upx
```

UPX is disabled by default: self-extracting binaries may be incompatible with some kernels,
virtualization environments or security policies. Pass `--upx` only after confirming the target
runtime supports it.

## Configuration

**Database** (`config.json`, or the `ARTEX_PG_DSN` environment variable):

```json
{
  "database": {
    "host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 5432,
    "user": "artex", "password": "yourpass",
    "dbname": "artex", "sslmode": "disable"
  }
}
```

**LLM**: `export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-...` (or `OPENAI_API_KEY`), or configure it in the UI's
"LLM Configuration" page, which can also add a local Ollama server as a keyless provider (format
"Ollama", default base URL `http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1`). Optional:
`ARTEX_LLM_PROVIDER` (`anthropic | openai | openai-responses | ollama`), `ARTEX_LLM_MODEL`,
`ARTEX_LLM_BASE_URL`, `ARTEX_LLM_PROXY`.

**Base URL gotcha**: for the Anthropic format, enter the host **without** `/v1` (for example
`https://api.anthropic.com`); ARTEX appends `/v1/messages`. OpenAI-format providers append
`/chat/completions` (or `/responses` for `openai-responses`), so their base **does** end in `/v1`
(for example `https://api.openai.com/v1`).

**Concurrency**: work agents per task, in "System Settings" (default 3).

**Untrusted-output boundary (on by default)**: tool results for the worker, planner, chat and main
agent are framed between nonce-tagged markers so the model treats them as data, not instructions.
Unset or empty, the boundary is on; set `ARTEX_UNTRUSTED_BOUNDARY=0` (or `false` / `off` / `no`) to
disable it. Cost: about 154 bytes per tool result plus one system note.

**Noise profile (off by default)**: `ARTEX_NOISE_PROFILE` paces the requests ARTEX sends to targets
(WebFetch, HTTP custom tools, the enrich probe). Unset or `off` keeps today's behaviour: no limit,
no cache. `quiet` = 2 req/s per host (burst 4, 1 in flight), `balanced` = 5 req/s (burst 10, 2 in
flight), `aggressive` = 20 req/s (burst 40, 4 in flight). A profile adds jitter, backs off on
429/503 (honours `Retry-After`, bounded retries, GET/HEAD/OPTIONS only), deduplicates identical
in-flight GETs and caches them briefly (60/30/10 s; never POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE), and logs a
per-host noise line each minute. `ARTEX_TARGET_USER_AGENT` sets a User-Agent on target requests
that carry none. Bash-launched tools are not paced yet; the low-and-slow prompt block supplies
their rate flags.

**Low-and-slow agent guidance (off by default)**: when a noise profile is set, the planner, worker,
main agent and chat agents receive a code-owned prompt block with the profile's per-host limits and
exact rate/delay flags for the installed scanners. It tells them to test one host at a time, back
off on 429/503 and never raise the rate to meet a deadline.

**Run budgets (off by default)**: `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TOKENS` / `ARTEX_TASK_BUDGET_TURNS` cap a
task's total spend (planner rounds and workers); `ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TOKENS` /
`ARTEX_INTENT_BUDGET_TURNS` cap one worker run. Unset or `0` means unlimited. A worker is not
started when the remaining task budget cannot cover its estimated cost (the average of finished
workers, else 50,000 tokens and 10 turns). Near the wrap-up reserve (the larger of 5% and 20,000
tokens, and 2 turns) the task enters a forced wrap-up: the planner writes a summary and final goal
judgment, and workers may only write back. The task then ends `done` if its goals are met, else
`timeout`. Practical floor: below 50,000 tokens no worker starts; 50,000-70,000 typically gives one
worker then wrap-up; pick well above 70,000 for real exploration.

**Common flags**: `./start.sh -addr :8787 -proxy :8788` (`-addr` frontend/API, `-proxy` traffic
recording proxy).

### Reverse proxy deployment (HTTPS / exposing only 443)

The frontend, API and SSE stream share port 8787 (the binary listens on `127.0.0.1:8787` by
default; the Docker container publishes on `127.0.0.1`), and the activity stream is same-origin by
default, so **no `NEXT_PUBLIC_SSE_BASE` is needed**: expose 443 and keep 8787 internal.

SSE keeps a long-lived connection with continuous pushes, so the proxy **must disable buffering**;
otherwise the browser connects but never receives events. Nginx example:

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name your.domain.com;
    # ssl_certificate / ssl_certificate_key ...

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8787;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;

        # SSE essentials: buffering off, long timeouts, HTTP/1.1
        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_cache off;
        proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
    }
}
```

**Login rate limit behind a proxy**: login allows 10 attempts per minute per client IP. Behind a
proxy every request comes from the proxy's address, so without further setup all users share one
budget and an attacker who fails 10 logins blocks everyone, admin included, for up to 15 minutes.
Keep the `X-Forwarded-For` line and set `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES` (comma-separated CIDRs, empty by
default) to the address ARTEX sees the proxy connect from:

- **nginx and ARTEX both on the host** (binary, `./start.sh`): the peer is `127.0.0.1`; start ARTEX
  with `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES=127.0.0.1/32`.
- **nginx on the host, ARTEX in Docker** (`docker-compose.yml`): the connection reaches the
  container from the Docker bridge gateway (a `172.x` address), not from `127.0.0.1`. Find it with
  `docker network inspect artex_default --format '{{(index .IPAM.Config 0).Gateway}}'` (the network
  is `<project directory>_default`), put `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES=<gateway>/32` in `.env`, then
  `docker compose up -d`.

For a peer in that list, ARTEX reads `X-Forwarded-For` from the right and takes the first address
that is not a trusted proxy; from any other peer the header is ignored. Trust only proxies you run:
a trusted peer can claim any client address.

> Only when SSE needs a different origin from the page (e.g. a dedicated subdomain) should you set
> `NEXT_PUBLIC_SSE_BASE` **at build time** (it is baked into the static bundle during `next build`;
> setting it at container runtime has no effect).

## Operations

### Backups

`scripts/backup.sh` dumps the Postgres database (and optionally the data directory) with
timestamped output and rotation:

```bash
scripts/backup.sh --with-data          # db dump + data/ archive, keep 14
scripts/backup.sh --keep 7             # db only, keep 7
```

Restore into a running stack:

```bash
gunzip -c backups/artex-db-<timestamp>.sql.gz | docker compose exec -T postgres \
  psql -U "$POSTGRES_USER" -d "$POSTGRES_DB"
```

Stored secrets (LLM API keys and proxies, MCP env, task credentials, notification channel config,
Brave/Tavily search keys, web search and global proxies, the execution spec of custom tools) are
encrypted in the database with the key in `keys/secret.key` (generated at first start, mode 0600,
next to `jwt.key`). **A database backup without that key cannot restore those secrets**: back up
`keys/` with the dump, separately. Deployments without a persistent disk set
`ARTEX_SECRET_KEY` (32 bytes, base64 or hex, e.g. `openssl rand -base64 32`). ARTEX refuses to start
when the database holds encrypted secrets and no key is available.

Daily cron example (03:20, operator crontab):

```
20 3 * * * cd /path/to/ARTEX && scripts/backup.sh --with-data >> backups/backup.log 2>&1
```

### Updating and upgrading

> Upgrading swaps the program and never touches data: the Postgres volume `pgdata`, `./data`
> (traffic index, task files, transcripts), `./keys` (`jwt.key`, `secret.key`) and `./skills` are
> preserved. **No manual database step is needed**: on every start ARTEX applies its embedded
> `schema.sql` baseline, then any pending numbered migration from `db/migrations/`, in order, each
> in its own transaction. Restarting the new binary is the upgrade. Back up `./data`, `keys/` and
> the database before upgrading.

**Update banner (opt-in, off by default)**: start ARTEX with `ARTEX_UPDATE_CHECK=1` to ask the
public GitHub releases API for the latest tag, at most once per 24 hours (cached in memory; a
failed check is not retried within that window). When the release is newer, the web UI shows a
dismissible strip linking to Releases. The request sends only `User-Agent: artex-update-check`.
Unset, ARTEX makes no update request and shows no banner.

#### Upgrading from a clone made before 2026-10-23

The repository history was rewritten that day to drop a personal email address from the commit
metadata. A clone made before then cannot fast-forward, and `./update.sh` now stops instead of
silently rebuilding stale code. Recover once, then upgrade normally:

```bash
git stash                 # only if you have local changes
git fetch origin
git reset --hard origin/main
git stash pop             # only if you stashed
```

Your data is unaffected: `./data`, the `pgdata` volume and `./skills` are not part of git history.

#### Option 1: one-click update script

```bash
cd ARTEX
./update.sh
```

The script optionally `git pull`s, then offers **① Docker update** (`docker compose build artex` →
`docker compose up -d artex`) or **② local build update** (rebuild the frontend static assets, then
recompile `./artex`; restart the process for it to take effect).

#### Option 2: Docker Compose (manual)

```bash
cd ARTEX
git pull
docker compose build artex
docker compose up -d artex
docker image prune -f            # optional
```

#### Option 3: prebuilt binaries

Download the new zip, stop the old process, overwrite `artex` and `skills/` (keep `config.json` and
`data/`), then restart:

```bash
cp -r <extracted dir>/skills ./ && cp <extracted dir>/artex ./
./start.sh
```

#### Option 4: build from source

```bash
git pull
cd web && npm ci && npm run build:static && cd ..
cp -r web/out server/webui/dist
CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags embedui -o artex ./cmd/artex
# restart ./start.sh
```

## Development

```bash
./dev.sh    # backend(:8787) + traffic proxy(:8788) + frontend next dev(:5173) → http://localhost:5173
```

- Backend: `go run ./cmd/artex` (without `-tags embedui`, the frontend is not embedded)
- Frontend: `cd web && npm run dev` (`/api` is reverse-proxied to the backend, with hot reload)
- Tests: `go test ./...`
- Mock preview (no backend): `cd web && NEXT_PUBLIC_MOCK=1 npm run dev`

## Architecture

ARTEX is an **LLM multi-agent-driven autonomous penetration testing system**: a Go monolithic
backend (with the Next.js UI embedded) + PostgreSQL. Agent capabilities come from the
[`norma`](https://github.com/Autumn-27/norma) SDK (`agentcore` / `tool` / `permission` / `harness` /
`memory` / `transcript`). At its core is the **dual-graph architecture**, plus two autonomy
mechanisms: **process-level information exchange between workers** and the **planner's multi-round
shared todolist**.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph FE["Frontend Next.js (go:embed embedded single binary)"]
    UI["Dashboard · Tasks · Assets · Coverage graph · Traffic · Workspace · System settings"]
  end
  subgraph SRV["server (Go net/http)"]
    API["REST /api/*  JWT auth  SSE"]
    ENG["engine scheduling loop"]
    MGR["Manager  task/engine/store lifecycle"]
  end
  subgraph AG["agent (norma SDK)"]
    GO["goals  goal decomposition + scope extraction"]
    PL["planner  the planner (sole intent generator)"]
    WK["worker  executor ×N"]
    MA["mainagent  human-in-the-loop"]
  end
  subgraph DB["PostgreSQL"]
    AGRAPH["Asset graph  assets / companies / task_scope"]
    EGRAPH["Exploration graph  exploration_nodes / anchors / activity"]
  end
  subgraph SUB["Supporting subsystems"]
    PROXY["Traffic recording proxy  MITM + CA tracing"]
    GUARD["guard / intercept  tool approval gate"]
    ENR["enrich  DNS / HTTP async enrichment"]
    EXT["MCP · skills · memory · report"]
  end

  UI -->|HTTP| API
  API --> MGR --> ENG
  ENG --> PL
  ENG --> WK
  API --> MA
  API --> GO
  PL --> DB
  WK --> DB
  MA --> DB
  GO --> DB
  WK -->|"Bash / HTTP fully traced"| PROXY
  WK --> GUARD
  WK --> ENR
  PL -.-> EXT
  WK -.-> EXT
  MA -.-> EXT
```

| Layer | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| **Frontend** | Next.js static export embedded via `go:embed`; tasks, assets, exploration and coverage graphs, traffic, human-in-the-loop chat |
| **server** | `net/http` routing, JWT auth, SSE; `Manager` owns tasks, engines and DB stores |
| **engine** | One `plannerLoop` + N worker goroutines per task; intent claiming, timeout/pause/drain |
| **agent** | goals / planner / worker / mainagent; `ToolSet` exposes the dual graphs as LLM tools |
| **db** | PostgreSQL persistence (pgx); embedded schema and numbered migrations applied at startup |
| **Supporting** | Recording MITM proxy, approval gate, async enrichment, MCP/skills/memory/report |

---

## Security

Please report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub Security Advisories; see
[SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

Operational security properties:

- **Secrets at rest**: LLM keys/proxies, MCP environment, task credentials, notification config,
  search keys, proxies, custom-tool execution specs and traffic evidence snapshots are encrypted
  with AES-256-GCM using `keys/secret.key` (or `ARTEX_SECRET_KEY`). ARTEX refuses to start when
  encrypted data exists and no usable key is available.
- **First-run claim**: `/setup` requires a one-time token printed at startup; the UI binds to
  `127.0.0.1` by default.
- **Login protection**: 10 attempts per minute per client IP, with `ARTEX_TRUSTED_PROXIES` for
  correct client attribution behind a reverse proxy.
- **Untrusted tool output**: framed as data for every agent by default (prompt-injection boundary).
- **Release integrity**: SHA-256 sums, CycloneDX SBOM and GitHub build provenance attestations for
  release archives.

# Reference — Auth, registration, user management (PHASE 1 §9/§10/§11)

## Account model
Exactly one admin — the first account, unique-constrained. Admin never minted
by invite; transfer CLI-only (`hive admin transfer`) behind current admin's passkey.

## Registration modes
`REGISTRATION_MODE`: `open` (localhost default) / `invite` (hosted default,
auto-flip on non-loopback bind) / `closed`. Mode shown on login screen.

## Invite tokens
- `hive_inv_` + 32 random bytes, base32. SHA-256 at rest. Plaintext shown once.
- Fields: label, max_uses (default 1), expires_at (default 7d), assigned role,
  revoke flag, created-by, timestamps.
- Redemption `/register?token=...`: validate + decrement in ONE transaction.
- Timing-safe compare, generic "invalid or expired" error, 5 attempts/min/IP, audit.
- Warning when REGISTRATION_MODE=open while unused tokens exist.

## Passkeys
Token gates creation only; passkey/FIDO2 enrollment follows immediately,
mandatory on hosted. Admin can reset a child's passkey.

## User states
active, suspended, disabled, pending. Disable kills live sessions immediately.
Actions: disable, suspend, reinstate, reset passkey, force re-enroll, delete,
extend invite.

## Usage
Per-child requests, tokens in/out, model, cost, daily rollup, date filter,
filtered logs. Flag over configurable daily spend threshold.

## Key source
`byok` (default, encrypted at rest) or `hosted` (admin grant, monthly cap).
Neither → child cannot send a prompt. Tag every request with its source.

## Teaming
Per-child toggle, default off. Joined admin sees screen + task state, messages
in-band, takes over. Persistent "admin is watching" indicator; child sees who
joined and when. Server enforces 4 concurrent joins max.

## Chat
Two tabs: `AI`, `Users`. Children see only admin; admin sees roster + unread.
Offline messages queue, deliver on return with send time. Unread badges.
Admin DMs pinned above AI in child's view when unread.

## Telegram
Per-user bot link, optional. Mirrors DMs both directions. `!ai` prefix routes
inbound to the agent; replies return to Telegram. One-click unlink.

## Remote
QR opens browser client, can start WebRTC screen share. Android foreground
service, reconnect on resume. View-only unless control granted; revocable
mid-session.

## Console/logs
Level filter, search, follow, export, clear, admin scoping. Never log secrets.

## Docs
README, TROUBLESHOOTING, HELP, CONTRIBUTING, TUTORIALS, API_DOCS, CHANGELOG, LICENSE.

# Reference — Skill format (PHASE 1 §7)

```yaml
---
name: port-sweep
description: Fast TCP port sweep of an in-scope host before enumeration.
version: 1.0.0
tags: [recon, tcp]
---

## When to use
Before service fingerprinting, on any host in scope.

## Steps
1. Run nmap -Pn -p- --min-rate 2000 against the target.
2. Feed open ports to the fingerprint step.

## Notes
Back off to 500 if the target rate-limits.
```

Skill upload validates this format and rejects on mismatch.
